{{Short description|Type of cryptographic algorithm}}
'''Knapsack cryptosystems''' are [[cryptosystem]]s whose security is based on the hardness of solving the [[knapsack problem]]. They remain quite unpopular because simple versions of these algorithms have been broken for several decades.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Schneier |first1=Bruce |title=Secrets and Lies |date=2004 |publisher=Wiley Publishing, Inc |isbn=978-0-471-25311-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/secretsliesdigit00schn/page/95 95] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/secretsliesdigit00schn/page/95 }}</ref> However, that type of cryptosystem is a good candidate for [[post-quantum cryptography]].{{citation needed|date=November 2017}}

The most famous knapsack cryptosystem is the [[Merkle–Hellman knapsack cryptosystem|Merkle-Hellman Public Key Cryptosystem]], one of the first [[public key cryptography|public key cryptosystems]], published the same year as the [[RSA cryptosystem]]. However, this system has been broken by several attacks: one from [[Adi Shamir|Shamir]],{{sfn|Shamir|1982}} one by Adleman,{{sfn|Adleman|1983}} and the ''low density attack''.

However, there exist modern knapsack cryptosystems that are considered secure so far: among them is Nasako-Murakami 2006.{{sfn|Nasako|Murakami|2006}}

Knapsack cryptosystems, when not subject to classical cryptoanalysis, are believed to be difficult even for quantum computers. That is not the case for systems that rely on [[Integer factorization|factoring]] large integers, like [[RSA (cryptosystem)|RSA]], or computing [[discrete logarithms]], like [[ECDSA]], problems solved in [[Time complexity|polynomial time]] with [[Shor's algorithm]].<ref>{{cite journal 
|arxiv=quant-ph/9508027 
|title=Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer 
|first=Peter |last=Shor 
|journal=SIAM Journal on Computing 
|year=1997
|volume=26 
|issue=5 
|pages=1484–1509 
|doi=10.1137/s0097539795293172
|s2cid=2337707 
}}</ref>
